content: Acetyl-CoA carboxylase 2, also referred to as ACC-beta or ACC2, is an enzyme in humans that is encoded by the ACACB gene. Acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC) is a complex, multifunctional enzyme system. It is a biotin-containing enzyme that catalyzes the carboxylation of acetyl-CoA to malonyl-CoA. This reaction represents the rate-limiting step in the synthesis of fatty acids. ACC-beta is believed to regulate fatty acid oxidation through the ability of malonyl-CoA to inhibit carnitine palmitoyltransferase I, which is the rate-limiting step in the mitochondrial uptake and oxidation of fatty acids. ACC-beta is thought to play a role in the regulation of fatty acid oxidation rather than in fatty acid biosynthesis. Recently, human acetyl-CoA carboxylase has emerged as a potential target for the development of new anti-obesity drugs. However, when the ACC2 gene was knocked out in mice, no significant changes in body weight were observed compared to normal mice. This finding suggests that drug-mediated inhibition of ACC2 may not be an effective strategy for treating obesity.
